title: Car Dealerships Are (Finally) Getting What They Deserve…

paras: On the night of June 18th, 2024, hackers broke into the software that runs a huge share of America's car dealerships.
The company was CDK Global.
About 15,000 dealerships across North America lost the system they use to sell, finance and service cars.
Six months later, the Federal Trade Commission and the state of Illinois reached a 20 million dollar settlement with a Chicago area dealer group.
It was the largest settlement the FTC had ever reached with a car dealer.
In September 2025, a Dallas used car dealer and lender called Tricolor collapsed into bankruptcy.
Its CEO was later charged with fraud.
And on October 1st, 2026, a new law in California gave used car buyers something new.
Three days to change their mind.
Here's the strange part.
Americans are paying more for a new car than ever.
In October 2026, the average one sold for 51,109 dollars.
And the dealer's profit on that car has collapsed.
This is the story of how car dealers made record money selling cars above the sticker price, where their money really comes from, and why the bill is finally coming due.
In January 2021, buying a new car worked the way it always had.
You negotiated.
The average buyer paid about 2,152 dollars below the sticker price, and fewer than 3 in 100 paid more than sticker.
Then the chips ran out.
A global shortage of computer chips slowed car factories to a crawl.
Dealer lots that used to be packed started to empty out.
For most businesses, empty shelves are a disaster.
For car dealers, it was the best thing that ever happened to them.
By January 2022, 82 percent of new car buyers were paying more than the sticker price, according to Edmunds.
On average, they paid 728 dollars over sticker.
A year earlier, the same buyers would have been haggling the price down.
The profits followed.
The dealers' own trade group, the National Automobile Dealers Association, reported that the average dealership's pretax profit more than doubled in the first nine months of 2021.
Look at AutoNation, one of the biggest dealer groups on the stock market.
In 2022, it made a gross profit of 5,942 dollars on every new car it sold.
Now the car itself was the jackpot.

sections.chapter: How a dealer really makes money
paras: But the car was never the whole business.
To see the rest, picture the moment after you agree on a price.
You shake hands with the salesperson.
And then someone walks you to a small office in the back.
That office is called finance and insurance.
It's where your loan gets written, and where you're offered the extras.
An extended warranty. Gap insurance. Paint protection. Tire and wheel coverage.
Here's what AutoNation earned in the third quarter of 2026.
Total gross profit was 1.21 billion dollars.
New cars, the thing in the showroom, brought in just 11 percent of it.
Used cars, about 9 percent.
That little office in the back brought in 29 percent.
And the service bay, oil changes and repairs and parts, brought in 51 percent.
Put that another way.
On every new car AutoNation sold that quarter, it made a gross profit of 2,176 dollars.
On the finance and insurance side, it made 2,698 dollars per vehicle.
The paperwork now earns more than the car.
The biggest piece of that paperwork is the loan.
Most dealers don't lend you their own money.
They send your application to a bank, and the bank quotes them a rate.
Then, as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau describes it, the dealer can raise that rate before it reaches you.
The bureau says this is typically called dealer markup.
And the lender shares part of that extra interest with the dealer.
Here's the honest part.
We looked for a public number on how often buyers get a marked up rate, and how big the markup is.
We couldn't find one. Dealers don't report it.
So here's a simple illustration instead.
In the third quarter of 2026, the average new car loan was 44,664 dollars, at 7 percent, for about 70 months, according to Edmunds.
By our math, that's a payment of about 780 dollars a month.
Add just one percentage point to that rate, and the payment rises by about 22 dollars.
Over the life of the loan, that's roughly 1,500 dollars more.
Most buyers watch the price of the car. Far fewer watch the price of the money.
And more of them are struggling to pay it.
Edmunds says 21 percent of new car buyers now pay at least 1,000 dollars a month.

sections.chapter: Fall number one: the markup is gone
paras: Fall number one: the markup is gone.
The factories caught up, and the lots filled back up.
By October 2026, dealers had 2.92 million new cars sitting on their lots, about 87 days' worth of sales, according to Cox Automotive.
Some brands were far worse.
In September, Jeep dealers had about 169 days of supply. Ram, about 152.
When the lot is full, the leverage flips back to you.
Automakers are paying more incentives again, about 3,490 dollars on the average new car in October.
And the dealer's slice keeps shrinking.
Remember AutoNation's 5,942 dollars per new car in 2022?
In the third quarter of 2026, it was 2,176.
That's a drop of about 63 percent.
Its net profit margin went from about 5 percent of revenue in 2022 to about 2 percent.
The tariffs didn't help.
On April 3rd, 2025, a 25 percent tariff on imported cars took effect.
Prices went up for buyers, while the dealer's profit on each car kept falling.
Fall number two came from the regulators.
In December 2023, the FTC finished a rule aimed squarely at car dealers.
It was called the CARS Rule.
It would have banned bait pricing, required dealers to give an all in offering price, and stopped them from charging for add-ons that give the buyer no benefit.
The FTC claimed it would save buyers 3.4 billion dollars a year.
The dealers sued.
And on January 27th, 2025, a federal appeals court threw the rule out.
Not because of what it said, but because the FTC had skipped a required step when it wrote it.
So the FTC went after dealers one at a time.
Leader Automotive, the Chicago group, was accused of charging for add-ons people didn't want and hiding junk fees.
It settled for 20 million dollars.
In March 2026, the FTC sent warning letters to 97 dealership groups about advertised prices that left out required fees.
In August, a Connecticut Nissan dealer agreed to pay 4 million dollars over claims that it double charged buyers for certified cars.
In October, the FTC said a Florida dealer group charged customers about 3,350 dollars above the advertised price in more than 92 percent of deals.
And in November, it settled with a Long Island lot whose ads promised, quote, no fees, no games.
To be clear, these are allegations and settlements, not court findings.
But California didn't wait for Washington.
Its new law, in effect since October 1st, 2026, lets buyers cancel the purchase of a used car priced at 50,000 dollars or less within three days, for a restocking fee.
Optional add-ons now have to be labeled optional, in writing.
And dealers can't sell an add-on that does nothing for the buyer, like an oil change plan on an electric car.
Fall number three is the borrowers.
Remember those 1,000 dollar payments?
Not everyone can keep making them.
In October 2025, the share of subprime auto loans at least 60 days past due hit 6.65 percent.
According to Fitch Ratings, that was the highest in data going back to 1994.
In 2024, Cox Automotive estimated about 1.73 million cars were repossessed, the most since 2009.
The businesses that sell to those buyers took the hardest hit.
Tricolor sold used cars in Texas and made the loans itself.
It filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy on September 10th, 2025, and shut down.
Federal prosecutors say it pledged the same car loans to more than one lender.
By August 2025, they allege, about 2.2 billion dollars of collateral had been pledged, against roughly 1.4 billion that actually existed.
Lenders were left owed more than 900 million dollars.
Its CEO, Daniel Chu, was charged in December 2025. He is presumed innocent, and the charges are accusations.
Two other former executives have pleaded guilty.
And America's Car Mart, a public chain that sells and finances used cars, lost more than 139 million dollars in its last fiscal year.
It warned there was substantial doubt it could continue as a going concern.
By its latest quarter, it had 94 stores, down from 154 a year earlier.
Now, the other side, because it matters.
Most dealers are not Tricolor.
There were about 17,000 franchised new car dealerships in America in 2025, and they employed more than 1.1 million people.
And the margins are thinner than most people think.
AutoNation kept about 2 cents of profit for every dollar of revenue last quarter.
The legal fight isn't one sided either.
The CARS Rule is gone.
And in October 2026, the FTC dropped its case against Asbury Automotive, one of the biggest dealer groups, without any ruling on the claims.
Dealers also argue they do real work.
They hold the inventory, take trade-ins, handle registration and run the service bays that keep older cars on the road.
And in many states, franchise laws still say new cars have to be sold through them.
And dealers have survived worse.
In May 2009, as Chrysler went through bankruptcy, it told 789 of its roughly 3,200 dealers they were finished.
The next day, GM said about 1,100 of its dealers would not be renewed.
The dealers' trade group warned that nearly 100,000 jobs were at risk.
Dealers took it to Congress, and by the end of that year, the ones who were cut had won the right to arbitration.
About a decade later, the dealers who made it through were posting record profits.
The lesson is simple. Dealers don't disappear. They adapt.

sections.chapter: So, did they get what they deserve?
paras: So, are car dealerships finally getting what they deserve?
Some of them are.
The markup years are over, and AutoNation's profit on each new car is down by almost two thirds.
The ones accused of hiding fees are paying settlements, and in California, buyers can now walk a used car back.
And the lenders who trusted Tricolor are still counting what's missing.
But the model itself is doing just fine.
At AutoNation, the service bay and the finance office together now bring in about 80 percent of the gross profit.
The new car out front brings in about 11.
Here's the number that sums it up.
On a car that costs 51,000 dollars, one of the biggest public dealer groups made more money on the paperwork than on the car.
The car isn't really the product. It's the reason you walk through the door.
So next time you buy one, check the price of the money, not just the price of the car.
Next on Money Encode: the 40 dollar oil change that's never 40 dollars.
